## Overview

The Business Formation Statistics (BFS) track applications for Employer
Identification Numbers (EINs) on IRS Form SS-4 as a leading indicator
of entrepreneurial intent. An EIN application is a signal of business
initiation — not proof that a new employer business was created. BFS
captures the earliest observable administrative step in the business
formation process, before applications become establishments, before
establishments create jobs, and before those jobs show up in
employment and wage data.

Understanding BFS in relation to the other datasets is key to using it
well: BFS shows where people are initiating businesses; BDS reveals
whether those applications become employer establishments and what job
dynamics follow; QCEW provides the resulting employment and wage picture.
Together, they describe the full progression from entrepreneurial intent
to labor market outcome.

The program's primary county-level series is the **Business Application
Series (BA)**, which captures a broad subset of EIN applications
associated with business initiation — excluding tax liens, estates,
trusts, certain financial filings, and applications in industries with
low transition rates to employer businesses. At the national and state level, BFS also publishes a
**High-Propensity Business Applications (HBA)** series — restricted to
applications more likely to become employer businesses — and **Projected
Business Formations (PBF)**, which estimates conversion rates within
four and eight quarters. These finer series are not available at the
county level.

## What This Data Tells Us About Rural America

Business formation statistics — tracking EIN applications as a leading
indicator of entrepreneurial intent — provide an early signal of
economic momentum that establishment counts and employment data can only
confirm after the fact. For rural communities, this leading-indicator
quality is particularly valuable: because business applications occur
before employer business formation and employment, changes in application
activity can provide earlier visibility into changing entrepreneurial
conditions than establishment and employment measures alone.

The pandemic-era surge in rural business applications also illustrates
why formation activity needs to be evaluated alongside subsequent
business formation and survival. A rise in applications does not
necessarily translate into durable establishment growth. Comparing BFS
with BDS can help identify where strong application activity was followed
by actual business formation and job creation — and where it was not.

## Coverage

- **Geography:** County, State, National
- **Time range:** Monthly data begin July 2004; annual county Business
  Application data begin 2005
- **Update frequency:** Monthly national and state data; annual county
  data typically released approximately six months after the reference
  year
- **Universe:** EIN applications on IRS Form SS-4, excluding tax liens,
  estates, trusts, agriculture (NAICS 11), and public administration
  (NAICS 92)

::: callout-note
**County data is BA only:** The Census county-level file contains the
Business Application (BA) series only. High-propensity (HBA) and
Projected Business Formation (PBF) series — which estimate how many
applications become employer businesses — are available at the national
and state level but not at the county level. County-level BFS tells us
where people are applying to start businesses; it does not provide
county-level estimates of which applications ultimately become employer
businesses.
:::

::: callout-important
**Mind the noise.** County-level BFS application counts are subject to
disclosure-avoidance procedures including differential privacy, with
geometric noise added to counts and subsequent calibration to state
totals. Small year-to-year changes in county application counts should
be interpreted with caution, particularly in very small counties. See
the [BFS methodology
page](https://www.census.gov/econ/bfs/methodology.html) for details on
the disclosure avoidance approach applied to county data.
:::

## Key Variables

Counts and rates answer different questions. Counts show the scale of
business application activity in a county; rates allow comparison of
entrepreneurial activity across communities of very different sizes.

- **Total business applications (BA)** — count of EIN applications
  meeting BFS coverage criteria; the primary county-level measure of
  business initiation activity
- **Applications per 1,000 population** — population-normalized rate
  for comparing application intensity across counties

## Accessing the Data

### Via CORI R Package

The [`cori.data.bfs`](/packages/cori-data-bfs/) package provides tidy
annual county-level access to BFS business application counts, with
population normalization via `cori.data.pep`.

```r
library(cori.data.bfs)

# All counties, all years
get_business_applications(geography = "county")

# Specific counties, recent years
get_business_applications(
  geoids = c("33009", "33011"),
  years  = 2010:2024
)
```

### Direct from Source

Monthly national and state data, and annual county files, are available
from the [BFS data page](https://www.census.gov/econ/bfs/data.html).
See the [BFS methodology
page](https://www.census.gov/econ/bfs/technicaldocumentation/methodology.html)
for documentation of the EIN application filtering process, the
high-propensity classification methodology, and the projected formations
estimation approach.

## Related

- **Package:** [cori.data.bfs](/packages/cori-data-bfs/) — CORI's
  tidy county-level access layer
- **Package:** [cori.data](/packages/cori-data/) — meta-package
  including `cori.data.bfs`
- **Dataset:** [Census Business Dynamics
  Statistics](/datasets/census-bds/) — provides observed establishment
  births, deaths, and job flows; pairing BFS with BDS helps assess
  whether increases in application activity are followed by actual
  employer business formation and job creation
- **Dataset:** [QCEW Employment &
  Wages](/datasets/qcew-employment-wages/) — provides current employment
  and wage levels, allowing researchers to connect earlier application
  trends to changes in the local labor market
- **Project:** [Rural Economic
  Outlook](/projects/rural-economic-outlook/) — BFS is an input to
  CORI's multi-dataset economic analysis
